title: Juvenile green turtles demonstrate developmental plasticity in a dynamic seascape
content:
Abstract
Organisms adopt life-history strategies that optimize growth, survival, and reproduction under varying environmental constraints. Understanding how these strategies vary across life stages is critical for ecological insight and ultimately effective conservation. Although the green turtle (Chelonia mydas) is one of the most widely studied marine turtle species, substantial gaps remain in our understanding of juvenile ecology within neritic foraging habitats, where environmental conditions—such as habitat quality, resource availability, and seasonal variability—can have lasting effects on growth, survival, and future reproductive potential. Still, no global synthesis has examined how such environmental variability shapes juvenile development. We conducted a structured global literature review with a thematic content analysis to synthesize current knowledge about juvenile green turtle foraging ecology—encompassing spatial use, diet, and foraging strategies—and associated developmental patterns. Drawing on 172 peer-reviewed studies published from 1979 to 2025; we identify key environmental drivers influencing foraging ecology and development. Our findings reveal substantial variation within and among populations, challenging traditional deterministic models of green turtle ontogeny. Juveniles function as facultative omnivores, with foraging strategies and developmental trajectories shaped by ecological context rather than fixed pathways. This variation reflects how individuals balance energy acquisition, expenditure, and habitat use under different environmental conditions, resulting in context-dependent growth responses rather than discrete or predetermined strategies. Within this context, three broad, non-exclusive growth-motivated strategies emerge: Resident Optimizers, Seasonal Responders, and Competition-Constrained Shifters, each reflecting different responses to environmental conditions and associated energetic constraints. By synthesizing global data, this review advances understanding of juvenile foraging ecology and reveals novel context-dependent, growth-motivated developmental strategies. We provide a foundation for future research and emphasize the need for flexible, regionally tailored conservation approaches that reflect the dynamic nature of juvenile green turtle development.
